newsitem.title: UK: Speculation about BOE's George worries markets.
newsitem.headline: Speculation about BOE's George worries markets.

text.p: Speculation that Bank of England Governor Eddie George might not be reappointed at the end of his five-year term next year is causing some anxiety on financial markets, economists said on Thursday.
George, nicknamed "Steady Eddie" for his hawkish anti-inflation views, is credited by many with piloting Britain to its best inflation performance for more than thirty years.

The new Labour government's decision to give the Bank of England the freedom to set interest rates makes George all the more important to the country's monetary policy and losing him could undermine the progress it has made.

"Until the new arrangements have proved their worth and established a visible track record in terms of control of inflation, the markets would view the early departure of Mr George with some concern," Morgan Stanley UK economist Kevin Gardiner said.
The Financial Times fuelled market rumours on Thursday by quoting unnamed senior government members as saying George might not be reappointed.

The newspaper said George's criticism on Wednesday of Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's decision to transfer the central bank's regulatory role to a strengthened Securities and Investment Board had played into the hands of members of the government who wanted to replace him.
George told the press conference that he had considered resigning, although not seriously, over Brown's decision.
"If the split is over banking supervision, it's less serious than if it's over monetary policy," said Salomon Brothers economist Michael Saunders.

"George does have a reasonable track record and that is important. He has usually been a little bit on the tighter side, but given inflation has been above the target for most of the period, he has sort of been vindicated."
The prospect of George, a Bank of England man through and through, being replaced with someone who could be seen as a political appointee, would also be viewed with concern.
The Financial Times, echoing the views of many in the City, said Goldman Sachs chief economist Gavyn Davies, a long-time Labour Party adviser, was the front-runner to succeed George.

It said Davies, widely tipped to become a deputy governor with a seat on the Bank's new monetary policy committee in the near future, had told Brown he would only accept a more junior position if assured that he would soon replace George.

Markets are already eagerly awaiting news of the make-up of the nine-member monetary policy committee and seeking reassurance that the Committee will have an in-built anti-inflation bias, not a political one.
The difficulty is acute for Labour, which is still regarded with some suspicion in business circles because of its history of presiding over rampant inflation.
Yamaichi chief economist John Shepperd believes the new government will try to avoid upsetting markets or undermining its own credibility through questionable appointments at the central bank.
"It is too obvious a trap for them to fall into and I'm sure they will avoid it," he said.

"It would be a pity if, having made this bold, historic move, they managed to undermine it by trying to slant the committee in a political way or losing someone who already has inherently the credibility they need."
